q: Who is credited with elaborating the "social representation theory"?

concept.t: Moscovici launched social representations theory in 1961 by studying how psychoanalysis became French common sense.
A new idea becomes common sense through anchoring (tying it to familiar categories) and objectification (turning it into a concrete image).

wrong.b: Known for work on social identity and his uncertainty-identity theory, not social representations.
wrong.c: With Mark R. Leary, proposed the need to belong (1995), a theory of motivation, not of shared common sense.
wrong.d: Proposed the sociometer theory of self-esteem and, with Baumeister, the need to belong (1995); the theorist is Mark R. Leary.

q: Which one refers to the behaviour that an individual engages in while enacting a role?

concept.t: Role playing (also called role enactment) is the actual behaviour of the person performing a role.
The stem asks for the behaviour shown while enacting a role: the doing, not the thinking or the expecting.

wrong.a: Mead's mental act of seeing a situation from another person's viewpoint; it is thinking, not behaving.
wrong.c: A young child's make-believe, pretending at a role rather than actually performing one.
wrong.d: What other people expect of the role occupant, not what the occupant actually does.

q: Some students experience an intense period of adaptation when they leave their old school environment and start college, especially during those initial days before they find companions, start to fit in and feel comfortable. This process is best described as:

concept.t: Resocialisation is unlearning old norms and roles and learning new ones.
It follows a major transition such as starting college: the student drops old-school ways and learns the new setting's.

wrong.a: Cooley's self-image built from others' imagined judgements of us, not adapting to a new setting.
wrong.b: Just attention turned on oneself; it says nothing about learning new norms.
wrong.c: The apathetic dependence of long-stay inmates on an institution, not fitting into a new life.

q: A tendency to act in a way that is consistent with one's own belief, expectation, or cognition about an event or behavior, thereby increasing the likelihood that the event or behavior will occur, is termed as:

concept.t: A self-fulfilling prophecy is acting on an expectation in ways that make it come true.
Merton coined the term in 1948. The belief changes behaviour, and the behaviour changes the outcome.

wrong.b: Only seeks evidence that fits a belief; it changes nothing in the world, so the event is not made more likely.
wrong.c: Not a recognised term in psychology; a made-up distractor.
wrong.d: Ignoring how common something is (its base rate) when judging likelihood.

q: What is the halo effect?

concept.t: In the halo effect, one salient positive trait or an overall impression colours ratings of unrelated traits.
Thorndike named it in 1920.

wrong.a: Stereotyping: judging a person by the group they belong to.
wrong.c: A consequence of a halo, not its definition; the halo is one trait spreading to others.
wrong.d: The primacy effect (or anchoring), where early information weighs most.

q: A teacher watches two students interact for less than a minute and correctly infers who is the class leader. This example best illustrates:
who: Ambady and Rosenthal, thin slices of behaviour

concept.t: Thin slicing is making accurate judgements from very brief samples of behaviour.
Ambady and Rosenthal showed that silent clips of 30 seconds or less yield accurate judgements.

wrong.a: Better performance of well-learned tasks in front of others; it is about performing, not judging.
wrong.b: The teacher's expectation did not create the leadership; the teacher only perceived it.
wrong.d: Over-explaining behaviour by disposition; here the brief judgement was accurate, not an error.

q: Arrange the process of communication in sequence

concept.t: The sender first encodes the idea into symbols, and the message travels through a channel.
It reaches the recipient, who then decodes it. So: encoding, channel, recipient, decoding.

wrong.a: Puts decoding before the message is sent through the channel or received.
wrong.b: Sends the message through the channel before it is encoded.
wrong.c: Starts with the channel and decodes before the recipient gets it, leaving encoding last.

q: The tendency of people to attribute their own behavior to external causes and other’s behavior to internal causes is referred to as :

concept.t: As actors we explain our own behaviour by the situation; as observers we explain others' by their dispositions.
Jones and Nisbett described it in 1971.
The stem contrasts self and others; only this effect covers both sides.

wrong.a: Concerns our own successes and failures, not the self-versus-other split in explaining behaviour.
wrong.b: Concerns only other people's behaviour; it has no self-versus-other contrast.
wrong.d: A generalised belief about a group, not an attribution pattern.

q: The "just-world hypothesis" explains victim-blaming as a result of:

concept.t: Melvin Lerner held that people need to believe the world is orderly, predictable and fair.
An innocent person's suffering threatens this belief, so observers restore it by deciding the victim deserved it.

wrong.a: Observers are distressed by the suffering, not sadistic; blaming defends their belief.
wrong.c: The dispositional blame is the result of the belief, not its cause.
wrong.d: Downward social comparison is a different process, not a defence of a belief in fairness.

q: Arvind is a college student who has strong negative feelings about smoking cigarettes. His grandfather died of lung cancer and he believes smoking is disgusting. One night at a party, Arvind's friends all go outside for a cigarette and he decides to smoke as well. What will he most likely experience as a result?

concept.t: Cognitive dissonance is Festinger's aversive tension felt when actions clash with beliefs.
Arvind acts against a strong, important attitude (smoking is disgusting), so he will feel this tension.

wrong.a: A different paradigm, effort justification: valuing what cost us effort; nothing here involved effort.
wrong.b: Nothing in the story suggests a stronger urge to smoke; he dislikes smoking.
wrong.d: Hull's motivation theory, not a reaction to acting against an attitude.

q: In which of the following scenarios would it be most difficult to predict behaviour from attitudes?

concept.t: Hearsay-based attitudes, formed by indirect experience, are weak and less accessible, so they predict behaviour poorly.
Regan and Fazio (1977) showed that direct experience strengthens the attitude-behaviour link.

wrong.a: High personal relevance strengthens the attitude-behaviour link, so prediction is easier.
wrong.c: More knowledge of the object strengthens the link, so prediction is easier.
wrong.d: Direct experience makes the attitude strong (Regan and Fazio, 1977), so prediction is easiest.

q: In Social Psychology, reactance is :

concept.t: Reactance is the motivation to restore a freedom when it is threatened.
Brehm (1966) defined it; it often makes the forbidden option more attractive.

wrong.a: That is compliance (complying with requests), the opposite of pushing back against a threat to freedom.
wrong.c: Persuasion: attitude change driven by a message.
wrong.d: Conformity, going along with group norms.

q: According to social identity theory, prejudice arises primarily due to :

concept.t: Tajfel's minimal groups showed in-group favouritism with no resources at stake.
So categorisation plus the need for positive distinctiveness is enough to produce prejudice.

wrong.a: Sherif's realistic conflict theory, not social identity theory.
wrong.b: Festinger's theory of inconsistent cognitions; unrelated to this account of prejudice.
wrong.d: Performance in the presence of others; unrelated to prejudice.

q: Low-prejudiced people engage in:

concept.t: Devine (1989) found stereotypes are activated automatically in high- and low-prejudiced people alike.
Low-prejudiced people then use controlled processing to inhibit the stereotype.

wrong.a: The first stage, common to all; low-prejudiced people go on to override it.
wrong.c: Pairs the processes wrongly: controlled processing is what inhibits stereotyping, not what produces it.
wrong.d: Pairs the processes wrongly: automatic processing gives involuntary, not voluntary, stereotyping.

q: The phenomenon where a qualified individual is prevented from advancing to higher positions in their career due to an invisible barrier based on gender or minority status is called:
who: Wall Street Journal article (1986), glass ceiling

concept.t: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier of attitudes and organisational bias near the top.
The term was popularised by a 1986 Wall Street Journal article.

wrong.a: Accumulated advantage (Merton, 1968), not a barrier to advancement.
wrong.c: Concerns impressions, not career barriers.
wrong.d: Concerns expectations, not career barriers.

q: 'The more we see and interact with a person, the more likely he or she is to become our friend or sexual partner.' This denotes:

concept.t: The propinquity effect: nearness and frequent interaction breed friendship.
Festinger, Schachter and Back (1950) showed this.

wrong.b: Narrower: mere repeated exposure to any stimulus raises liking; it is the mechanism behind propinquity.
wrong.c: Choosing partners of similar attractiveness.
wrong.d: Liking those who like us.

q: Emotional isolation means:
who: Robert Weiss (1973), emotional versus social isolation

concept.t: Robert Weiss (1973) separated emotional isolation from social isolation.
Emotional isolation is lacking a deep attachment to one specific person; social isolation is lacking a wider network of friends and associates.

wrong.b: This is social isolation, Weiss's other type.
wrong.c: Incompetence is a correlate of loneliness, not one of its types.
wrong.d: Low self-esteem is a correlate of loneliness, not one of its types.

q: Which concept is closely related to FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) in social media research?

concept.t: FOMO (Przybylski and colleagues 2013) arises from constant upward comparison with others' curated experiences.
It sits in the tradition of Festinger's social comparison theory (1954).

wrong.b: A learning process, not comparison with others.
wrong.c: A learning process, not comparison with others.
wrong.d: A consistency process, not comparison with others.

q: Which of the following is an example of the power of roles?

concept.t: Students randomly made guards or prisoners took on their roles so fully that the study was stopped after six days.
Ordinary people changed because of the role they were given: the power of roles.

wrong.a: Studied intergroup conflict (Robbers Cave), not the power of roles.
wrong.b: Was the small-world study, not a study of roles.
wrong.c: Dr Zilstein was the fictitious experimenter of Schachter's affiliation study, not research on roles.

q: What is normative social influence?

concept.t: Normative social influence is going along with others out of the desire to be accepted and liked.
Deutsch and Gerard (1955) contrasted it with informational influence, the desire to be correct.

wrong.a: Informational influence, the other half of Deutsch and Gerard's pair.
wrong.c: Describes internalisation (personal values), not influence from others' approval.
wrong.d: Describes obedience.

q: According to Cialdini, techniques for gaining compliance rest to a large extent on six basic principles. These do NOT include:

concept.t: Cialdini's six are reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social validation (social proof), friendship or liking, authority and scarcity.
Reward is not on the list.

wrong.a: One of the six: things seem more valuable when they are rare or running out.
wrong.b: One of the six, also called social proof: we follow what others are doing.
wrong.c: One of the six: we say yes more readily to people we know and like.

q: The bystander effect, where the presence of others inhibits helping, is primarily explained by two factors:

concept.t: Latané and Darley's first mechanism: each bystander assumes someone else will act.
Their second: each bystander reads the others' calm as a sign that nothing is wrong.
The other pairs are group phenomena of other kinds (Sections 3.6, 3.7 and 3.10).

wrong.a: Social loafing (slacking in a group effort) and deindividuation (losing self-awareness in a crowd) do not explain failing to help.
wrong.c: Social comparison (judging ourselves against others) and normative influence (conforming to be liked) are broader processes, not the two named mechanisms.
wrong.d: Group polarisation (discussion pushing views to extremes) and groupthink (cohesive groups suppressing dissent) concern group decisions, not helping.

q: A state that occurs when bystanders in an emergency situation use the behaviour of others to determine whether help is actually required is called:

concept.t: In an emergency, bystanders look to one another to decide whether help is needed.
Seeing calm faces, each wrongly concludes help is not needed: pluralistic ignorance.

wrong.b: Conformity: yielding to group pressure, not misreading others' calm in an emergency.
wrong.c: Compliance: yielding to a direct request.
wrong.d: The collective action of a large gathering, not bystanders reading one another.

q: Altruistic Personality is characterized by:

concept.t: The altruistic personality is a stable tendency to help across situations.
Bierhoff, Klein and Kramp (1991) found them to be empathy, belief in a just world, social responsibility, internal locus of control and low egocentrism.

wrong.a: Helping only when in the mood is situational helping, not a stable trait.
wrong.c: Cost-benefit calculation describes situational helping, not a stable trait.
wrong.d: Readiness only in emergencies describes situational helping; the trait shows across situations.

q: Who reformulated the "frustration-aggression hypothesis"?

concept.t: Leonard Berkowitz (1989) said frustration leads to aggression only to the extent that it produces negative affect.
Aggressive cues in the setting then tip the balance.

wrong.a: Dollard and colleagues proposed the original hypothesis (1939), not the reformulation.
wrong.b: Only softened the original (1941); the full recasting came later from Berkowitz.
wrong.d: Richard Lazarus is known for appraisal and stress, not aggression.

q: Albert Bandura's Bobo doll experiment is a classic demonstration of:

concept.t: Children copied an aggressive adult's specific acts toward the doll.
They were never reinforced, so the learning came from watching a model.

wrong.a: No reinforcement was given, so it is not operant conditioning.
wrong.c: Conditioned fear is the Little Albert study, not Bobo doll.
wrong.d: Studied in the McGill isolation research, not Bobo doll.

q: Low levels of which neurotransmitter leads to aggression

concept.t: Low serotonin activity is linked to impulsive aggression.
It appears as low 5-HIAA, a serotonin breakdown product, in cerebrospinal fluid.

wrong.b: Concerns reward and movement, not this aggression link.
wrong.c: Marks arousal in any strong emotion, not aggression in particular.
wrong.d: Like epinephrine, marks arousal in any strong emotion, not aggression in particular.

q: Which of the following is not a stage of group formation?

concept.t: Tuckman's stages are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
Proximity is a cause of interpersonal attraction, not a stage of group development.

wrong.a: A real stage, the second: conflict over roles and leadership.
wrong.c: A real stage, the third: the group settles its norms and cohesion.
wrong.d: A real stage, the fourth: the group gets on with its task.

q: Tim would like to participate in his high school's musical. He has been taking vocal lessons for years and is an excellent singer, but does not have much experience as a dancer. The director gives him a part where he has to sing and dance. Based on the theory of social facilitation, how will the presence of an audience affect Tim's performance?
who: Zajonc, drive theory of social facilitation

concept.t: By Zajonc's drive theory, an audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response.
The dominant response is correct on a well-learned task (singing) and often wrong on an unpractised one (dancing).

wrong.a: Reverses the prediction: arousal helps the well-learned task (singing) and hurts the unpractised one (dancing).
wrong.b: Ignores that the effect depends on how well learned the task is; his dancing is unpractised.
wrong.d: Ignores that the effect depends on how well learned the task is; his singing is well practised.

q: A group of scientists is deciding on the use of live animals in research; most of the group has used live animals. How might the leader reduce groupthink?

concept.t: Janis's remedies include a devil's advocate or critical subgroup.
Asking a subset to critique animal research builds in the dissent that groupthink suppresses.

wrong.a: Team-building raises cohesion, which worsens groupthink.
wrong.b: A leader stating views first steers the group, which worsens groupthink.
wrong.d: Forbidding argument suppresses dissent, which worsens groupthink.

q: Defense attorneys often protest the prosecutor's use of eyewitness testimony because:

concept.t: A source error is remembering a face but placing it in the wrong context.
A face met elsewhere (a mugshot, the news, a bystander) is misattributed to the crime.

wrong.a: Witnesses are not unusually forgetful.
wrong.b: False: confidence predicts accuracy only weakly and grows after feedback.
wrong.d: Eyesight is rarely the issue.

q: Which of the following is not a part of the social case work process?
who: Stages of the social case work process

concept.t: Case work runs intake and study, assessment (social diagnosis), treatment or intervention, evaluation, termination and follow-up.
Content analysis, coding themes in texts, is a research technique, not a case work step.

wrong.b: A real stage: treatment or intervention, which follows assessment.
wrong.c: A real stage, also called social diagnosis.
wrong.d: A real stage, coming before termination and follow-up.

q: Who among the following established group work as a method within the profession of social work?
who: Grace Coyle, Social Process in Organized Groups (1930)

concept.t: Grace Coyle's Social Process in Organized Groups (1930) founded group work as a method.
Link each name to one method: Richmond with case work, Coyle with group work.

wrong.a: Founded case work, not group work.
wrong.b: Wrote Common Human Needs; she did not establish group work.
wrong.d: Konopka carried group work into treatment settings later, building on it rather than establishing it.
